chunks: What they say here is that the disbeliever is blamed for himself, because God has established for him the proof for knowledge and enabled him to reach it,
so if he does not look and does not recognize, he is blamed for that by himself, and it is not blameworthy to hold him accountable,
likewise we say: the extending of the Imam's hand (authority), even if it escapes the duty-bound, is only due to himself;
and if he had enabled him, he would have appeared and his hand would have extended, and his grace would have materialized, so it would not be blameworthy to hold him accountable.
For the proof is against him, not for him. And we have fully covered similar cases in the place to which we referred, and we will mention them later if the need arises to mention them.

key_terms.الْكَافِرَ: The disbeliever or one who fails to recognize
key_terms.الْمُكَلَّفَ: The duty-bound (one subject to religious obligations)
key_terms.انْبِسَاطُ يَدِ الْإِمَامِ: The extending of the Imam's hand (metaphor for his authority and governance)

ai.seo_question: Why is the Imam's occultation not considered a failure of divine justice or a reason to absolve believers of religious duties?
ai.summary: Al-Tusi employs the principle of *al-hujja 'alayhi la 'alaih* (the proof is against the individual, not the Imam) to justify the validity of *taklif* (religious obligation) during the Major Occultation. He argues that since God provided the necessary signs and capacity for recognition, the failure to access the Imam's spiritual grace (*lutf*) is due to the individual's own negligence, thereby preserving the justice of divine command.
